articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Yvette Tan 
- Published 8 October 2026 
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries. 
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul. 
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place. 
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea. 
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter. 
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports. 
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions". 
"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said. 
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly". 
- 
Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
- Published 11 January 2025 
- 
Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll 
- Published 7 May 
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive". 
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security. 
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang. 
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war. 
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer. 
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement. 
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations. 
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war. 
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks. 
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment. 
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take. 
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US. 
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

articles.title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
articles.summary: The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations.
articles.full_text:
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Rajapaksa was arrested two days after returning to Sri Lanka from Singapore By BBC Sinhala   and   Yvette Tan 
- Published 7 October 2026 
Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital. 
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday. 
They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital. 
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government. 
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated. 
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October. 
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred. 
Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president. 
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine. 
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled. 
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family. 
Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand. 
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

articles.title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
articles.summary: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia correspondent 
- Published 6 October 2026 
At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. 
With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. 
Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. 
The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. 
"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. 
He has little doubt they are dead. 
But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave 
Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. 
Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. 
Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death. 
But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. 
"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. 
He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. 
For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. 
When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods 
Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. 
Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. 
Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. 
The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. 
The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. 
Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. 
Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. 
"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. 
He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. 
For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief 
The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. 
This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. 
The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. 
Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. 
"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." 
The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. 
In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. 
The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn). 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing 
At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. 
Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. 
Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. 
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. 
This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. 
For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. 
He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. 
But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. 
Once again, he is without a home. 
"I have lost everything," he said. 
So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. 
Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. 
He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home. 
Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari

articles.title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
articles.summary: The US Defence Secretary says the execution will be public, but a legal expert says the "unprecedented" decision is on "uncertain legal terrain".
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Sareen Habeshian 
- Published 8 October 2026 Updated 22 minutes ago 
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said. 
A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed. 
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death. 
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." 
Image source, Bell County Sheriff's Office/Reuters Image caption, 
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012 
The Pentagon had announced earlier this week that it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years. 
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be". 
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd." 
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said on Monday that the defence secretary had made the recommendation and Trump approved it. 
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution. 
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two. 
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted in court that he was the gunman in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. 
The shooting on 5 November 2009 took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. 
At court Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan. 
- 
Fort Hood attacker to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two 
- Published 1 day ago 
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgment on its legality to move forward. 
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution. 
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened. 
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added. 
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision". "To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he added. 
Fiddel said Hasan could pursue legal action that could trigger a lengthy legal process. 
"If he does exercise the right, the legal proceedings would last years," Fidell said. "They'd last far longer than President Trump's term in the White House," he added. 
Figure caption, 
Public execution is 'out of the Middle Ages', says Yale professor 
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses. 
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods. 
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says. 
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore." 
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-redistricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing. 
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content. 
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly. 
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. 
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows. 
While Trump has never publicly advocated for a public execution, he has long supported the death penalty. In 1989, for example, he took out large ads in The New York Times calling for the execution of the Central Park Five - who had been convicted of rape and assault charges but were later exonerated. 
Trump has previously condemned public executions in Iran, and has cited the Iranian government's potential killing of protesters as a possible justification for military intervention before attacking the country earlier this year. 
The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when the government conducted a flurry of 13 executions. 
Upon returning to office last January, Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions and signed an executive order aimed at "restoring" the death penalty and "protecting public safety". 
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency. 
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the World War Two.

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
articles.summary: A new film paints the Meta founder as a villain. But the tech firm seems immune to bad publicity, writes our North America tech correspondent.
articles.full_text:
By Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent 
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful. 
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make." 
Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists. 
It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company. 
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users. 
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case. 
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him. 
Image source, Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
This year Meta unveiled Muse, its AI companion app, alongside a Tamagotchi-like wearable device that allows users to talk to it 
His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned". 
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole. 
But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant. 
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it? 
Meta's 'trust deficit' 
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta. 
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users. 
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed. 
And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube. 
Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution. 
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases. 
Image source, CTMG, Inc./Leah Gallo Image caption, 
Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to one review of The Social Reckoning 
In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant. 
And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes. 
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users. 
Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight. 
Image source, Godofredo A. VÁSQUEZ / AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Meta faces lawsuits over its handling of young social media users. Outside one case in California this summer, protesters highlighted the names of young people they say died as a result of social media harms. Meta disputes many of the claims 
To some, the trust issue feels existential 
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business. 
"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover." 
'Withstanding the blowback' 
But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025. 
While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users. 
And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month. 
One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company. 
"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy. 
Meta's new AI agent 
However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust. 
Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time). 
It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet. 
But Muse works best when users hand over some of their most personal information to the company, including credit card information, purchase histories and access to email inboxes. 
It's a big ask for a company whose reputation on privacy has been sullied, starting a decade ago with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which followed the revelation that the data of millions of Facebook users was breached and used by a political consulting firm. 
Image source, Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty Images Image caption, 
Zuckerberg launched Facebook in 2004, aged 19, while studying at Harvard University 
Just two days after Zuckerberg's keynote at Meta Connect, another New Mexico jury found Meta lied about how Facebook used personal information. (The company has said it disagrees with the verdict and will defend itself against what it says are efforts to distort its record.) 
So are customers willing to hand over that data for the convenience of using Muse? 
Some users say yes. Since its launch one month ago, Muse already has more than five million downloads and more than three million weekly active users - outpacing the adoption of ChatGPT when that was first introduced, in the North American market. 
Zuckerberg has laid out a vision in which Muse couples with an ever-expanding line-up of Meta AI smart glasses, enabling users to summon hands-free what he calls "personal superintelligence". 
Meta clearly has big plans for its smart glasses. "I think they're making an investment to position themselves as a category leader," says Kate Winick, principal analyst at Forrester, covering social media and influencers. "However big this category turns out to be, they will own it - for now." 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Zuckerberg attended President Trump's inauguration ceremony last year, along with Elon Musk and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos 
The glasses are divisive, and have been labelled by some as "pervert glasses" because they can be used to film covertly. The company has moved to stop users from tampering with the light that indicates a photo or video is being captured. Zuckerberg also just announced new audio-only smart glasses, an apparent bid to quell privacy concerns. 
But the company's most strident critics remain wary. 
"Consumers know that Meta has problems, and that to date we haven't been able to trust them to make their products safe for children. So why would a consumer want to trust them with some of their most private and sensitive information?" says Brooke Istook of the Heat Initiative, a campaign group. 
Privacy versus convenience 
In his speech, Zuckerberg briefly addressed the sensitive issue of privacy. At one point during his talk, an image flashed on the screen behind him of its Muse mascot embracing a blue padlock. 
"Given how personal Muse and the content on your glasses is, we designed state-of-the-art privacy and security into all these systems from the beginning," Zuckerberg told the audience. 
He touted a personal virtual machine, for example - essentially a self-contained computer system running inside Meta's cloud, where it says Muse users' data will be stored. Zuckerberg promised it would keep every customer's information secure, and that soon "even Meta won't be able to see that information". He said the virtual machine will be launched later this year, with further privacy protections coming. 
Meta's focus on privacy and security seems aimed at reassuring consumers. But Winick says users still have to opt into many of those protections. "I think if they thought they could get away with not doing that, they would," she says. 
Not long after Zuckerberg took the stage in California, social media users started reporting cases of Muse running amok, including claims that the agent read emails without permission. Meta has pushed back against these reports, saying it does not believe that Muse accesses emails unless a user has consented. 
Image source, Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Campaigners celebrated in Los Angeles earlier this year after hearing that a US jury found Meta and YouTube liable in a social media addiction trial 
In the end, the bulk of users may be willing to make some concessions on privacy if it means convenience and utility, says Moorhead. "If the consumer sees the trade-off as beneficial, then they'll keep it going," he says. "This is why Facebook and Instagram still have billions of users." 
On the financial front, the social media advertising business – its cash cow – routinely brings in significant revenue. Meta reported $60.8bn in revenue and $15.9bn in profit for the second quarter of this year. 
Consistent profits have helped fuel bets from the much-mocked Metaverse , to its current mass expansion of AI infrastructure. 
And on Muse? "It's a very real time-saving benefit that a lot of people will want and will like," says Winick. 
AI investment is not cheap. Meta has now taken on $83.7bn in long-term debt, according to its most recent financial statement. 
Still, Meta executives are bullish about the company's pivot to AI. "It's really about your agent, who can do work on your behalf, who is your constant ally in whatever you're trying to accomplish in your goals in your life," Andrew Bosworth, the company's chief technology officer, said in an interview with the BBC. 
Meta has big plans. But its future may ultimately depend on whether its users can trust it.

articles.title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
articles.summary: Wicknell Chivayo divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Zanu-PF Image caption, 
Wicknell Chivayo, who had a fleet of personalised luxury cars, loved white Rolls-Royces By Ish Mafundikwa Reporting from Harare 
- Published 8 October 2026 
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death. 
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes. 
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving. 
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes. 
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality. 
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank. 
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people. 
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders. 
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures. 
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell. 
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death , external , explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts. 
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Wicknell Chivayo's death last week has dominated conversation in Zimbabwe 
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10. 
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis. 
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended. 
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts. 
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation. 
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career. 
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid. 
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment. 
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle. 
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day. 
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it. 
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power. 
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo. 
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company. 
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa. 
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF. 
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term. 
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing. 
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030. 
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote. 
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption , external : "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550". 
Image source, Zanu-PF Image caption, 
President Mnangagwa (L), seated next to Chivayo, was the guest of honour at a big apostolic church gathering in August 
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch , external . 
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu , external , Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan , external , Malawi's Peter Mutharika , external , Mozambique's Daniel Chapo , external , Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema , external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa , external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year. 
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home. 
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat , external . True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest." 
Ruto wrote on X following the death , external : "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent." 
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death. 
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it , external , listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan." 
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration" , external . 
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!" 
Image source, @sir_wicknell Image caption, 
Chivayo shared a clip of Kenya's President William Ruto driving him and his wife to their helicopter after his daughter's engagement 
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days. 
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying. 
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked. 
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing." 
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party. 
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive. 
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years. 
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us." 
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars. 
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes. 
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Veteran musician Thomas Mapfumo, who had turned down Chivayo's offer of gifts, was due to perform at the tycoon's birthday party in November 
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash. 
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty". 
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November. 
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician. 
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools. 
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him. 
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious. 
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement. 
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday. 
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic. 
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners. 
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts. 
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare
